As a result of negotiations, Russia rescinded an order of April 20, 1931, which had prohibited all importing organizations and trade representatives of the Soviet Union from purchasing any goods of Canadian origin, as well as from chartering Canadian vessels. Canada, on her part, rescinded the Order-in-Council of February 27, 1931, prohibiting the importation from the Soviet Union of coal, wood-pulp, pulpwood, lumber, asbestos and dressed furs.
A provisional trade agreement was concluded with Germany on October 22, 1936, whereby each country conceded to the other
a guarantee of most-favoured-nation treatment

in tariff matters. Associated with this was a "payments agreement," which provides that exchange accruing from German exports to Canada shall be made available for the purchase of Canadian goods. Definite percentages of this exchange are allotted for the purchase of commodities of such interest to Canada as wheat, apples, cheese, honey, fish, fox skins, asbestos and lumber.
The Canadian-Polish convention of commerce was brought into operation, providing for exchange of most favoured nation treatment between Canada and Poland, and for special concessions on both sides with respect to a limited list of articles.
A former arrangement with Brazil, whereby Canada conceded her intermediate tariff to Brazil in return for most favoured nation treatment, was terminated by Brazil on July 30, 1936, in pursuance of her policy of cancelling all old trade agreements. Following negotiations, Canada retained the benefit of the Brazilian minimum tariff (which is about one-quarter less than the maximum) on all goods, in return for granting to Brazil the Canadian intermediate tariff.
With another South American country, Uruguay, Canada signed an agreement on August 12, 1936, which provides for exchange of most-favoured-nation treatment as regards customs duties and related questions, including quotas and allocation of exchange for commercial transactions. Uruguay is to accord Canada her normal tariff, thus ensuring Canadian goods against a tariff one-half higher, which, under Uruguayan tariff regulations, may be applied to countries not offering reciprocity.
The trade agreement of 1932 between Canada and New Zealand, which was drawn for only one year, has been kept in operation by several renewals; on July 22, 1936, the agreement was extended until September 30, 1937, without further amendment.

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement
These general observations regarding the expansion of our import and export trade constitute a fitting introduction to the presentation to parliament of the new trade agreement which has just been concluded with the United Kingdom. The speech from the throne intimated that agreement in principle had been reached between the two governments. As you now know, sir, the new trade agreement was signed on Tuesday of this week, and at the conclusion of these remarks I shall lay it upon the table of the house.	At this point I should state that
by arrangement with the government of the United Kingdom, which is as anxious as we are to put the tariff changes arising from the agreement into force at the earliest possible moment, it has been agreed that the provisions of article 9 and schedule "E" of the 1932 agreement shall cease to have effect from 12 o'clock to-night, when the provisions of articles 6, 7, and 8 and schedules IV and V of the new agreement will be in effect.
The extent and importance of Canada's trade with the United Kingdom would enable me to give a much more imposing statistical presentation than I used earlier in these remarks. But in this matter widely known and well understood facts make mere figures seem superfluous. We all realize that Canada's most prized market has been and continues to be the United Kingdom. Every Canadian minister of finance, in almost every budget speech, has had occasion to refer to that fact. In going last summer to London to initiate the negotiations which have resulted in the agreement to be tabled this afternoon, Canadian ministers realized that they were setting out upon a mission the objective of which was not to capture but to hold the most valuable market this dominion has ever known. As to how or when or by whom that great market was gained for Canada is not a matter about which we need dispute. Former Liberal administrations were pioneers in seeking it out and securing it, for they first conceived and put into operation the principle of giving to British goods a preferred position in our economy. But the good work initiated in 1897 has been carried on by all succeeding governments in Canada, however greatly the views of the major parties might differ as to the best means of attaining the objective. While those of us who sit now to your right, Mr. Speaker, may not adopt the same methods as our predecessors, believing our own to be better, we readily admit that they and we have been and are actuated by a keen desire for the best good
of our country. Our objective, may I lepeat, at London last summer was to retain for Canada a magnificent market; and I am certain that the opinion of this house and the country will be that the ground which has been won over many years has been held and consolidated at a minimum of cost.
Time will permit me to review only briefly the general principles underlying the agreement and to summarize its main provisions. Needless to say, all the articles in the agreement as well as the items comprising the schedules thereto, will be open to the fullest discussion when the House is in committee.
Careful examination of the provisions of the new agreement, which can only be made in committee, will I think, convince the house that a successful effort has been made to bring the policy of British preference, which successive Canadian governments have maintained for forty years, into closer alignment with the trade policy to which this government stands committed. The present agreement is in no sense a simple renewal of the trade agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom signed at Ottawa in 1932. The detailed differences between it and the one which it will supersede will be developed in committee. From the beginning, however, it should be clearly understood that throughout the negotiations which resulted in the present agreement, the Canadian government has insisted on broadening the opportunities of international trade, without impairing the practical effectiveness of the British preferential system, and has endeavoured to apply within that system the principles of commercial policy which it hopes to see realized in the economic relations of Canada with the rest of the world. The measure in which these objectives, which were in large part shared by the government of the United Kingdom, have been attained, can only be appreciated by a close examination of the text of the new agreement and its comparison with the corresponding provisions of the Ottawa agreement of 1932.
The goal of both the United Kingdom and the Canadian government in intra-imperial, as in international trade, is the lowering of tariff barriers and the freeing of trade from fettering restrictions; and the preamble to the agreement is evidence of a new emphasis on the importance of increasing the volume of international and intra-imperial trade, and a departure from some of the earlier forms of preferential policy, which were too much concerned with diverting a diminishing volume of trade into unfamiliar and uneconomic channels.
The Budget-Mr. Dunning

An examination of the changes in the structure of the Canadian tariff resulting from the application of the provisions of the new agreement will show that the emphasis on trade expansion in its preamble is not misplaced. Although actual margins of preference on 179 items enumerated in schedule IV will be increased, in each case this increase is a consequence of a reduction in the duty against the United Kingdom. No preferences have been enlarged or created by increasing rates of duty against third countries, and the concessions made to the United Kingdom have been by way of lowered duties. It should not be necessary to stress the fundamental difference between this approach to the problem of preferential treatment and that which resulted in the 1932 agreement, in which a large proportion of the preferences guaranteed to the United Kingdom were created by raising the intermediate and general tariffs, and coupled, in a number of cases, with higher duties against the United Kingdom itself than had formerly been in force.
It will be found, in comparing the tariff items in schedule IV on which the preferential rate is reduced, with those in schedule I of the Canada-United States trade agreement, in which special reductions below the intermediate tariff were accorded the United States, that there are very few items which occur in both schedules. The explanation of the fact that enumerated tariff concessions to the United Kingdom and to the United States are largely made on different commodities lies in the complementary rather than competitive character of the bulk of Canadian imports from our two chief customers and sources of supply.
The reduction in the number of tariff items on which margins of preference are bound against decrease, from 215 in the 1932 agreement to 91 in schedule V of the present agreement, is further evidence of the effort that has been made to reconcile the principle of preferences with the necessity of removing barriers that stood in the way of international trade. The new agreement achieves a radical and far-reaching revision of the restrictions which its predecessor put upon the freedom of Canada to negotiate for the reciprocal reduction of tariff rates with third countries. Many items on which the differential margin between the British preferential and intermediate tariffs had operated either to limit Canadian trade treaty negotiations with foreign countries, to maintain prices of imported or domestic goods at unduly high levels, or in which five years' experience had shown that United Kingdom industries had not made, or were not likely to make, full use of the preferences

afforded them, have been dropped from the schedule, and, in twenty-one cases, the margins of preference on items remaining have been reduced.
In addition to the limited number of fixed margins of preference provided for in schedule V of article 8, there is provision in article 7 for a sliding margin of preference on United Kingdom goods, which are enumerated in schedule IV, dutiable under that schedule and " not of a class or kind made in Canada." I might point out that the obligation to maintain preferential margins on goods in this special category is terminable at any time by the reduction of the British preferential rate to free entry.
Further, either government is free at any time to modify or suspend any of the margins of preference set out in schedules III or V, if it is satisfied that a combine or monopoly of exporters is exploiting its domestic consumers by virtue of the preferential margins there provided for.
The gradual change and diversification of trade between Canada and the United Kingdom has given a very real point to the grievance frequently voiced by British industrialists who have been heard to complain that while competitive Canadian goods could enter the British market free of ordinary duty and free of dumping duty, and in some cases be sold there at prices below the fair market value for home consumption of the same goods in Canada, if the British manufacturer tried to meet dumping by dumping, his efforts were effectively blocked by ordinary duty plus special duty, which kept the Canadian market a closed and profitable preserve for our protected manufacturers. Such situations I know were not very frequent, but that they could occur is sufficient justification for the inclusion in the agreement of a special provision- article 12-under which the Canadian government agree that, in circumstances such as I have described, they will exempt particular classes of United Kingdom goods from dumping duty. This article is self-explanatory; it will, I think, be recognized as neither more nor less than an assurance of fair play both for the British manufacturer and the Canadian consumer. I hope that this evidence- afforded by the presence of this article in the agreement-of the government's determination to give no shelter or protection to unfair practice in export or internal trade, will in itself lead offenders to abandon the practice complained of, and make it unnecessary to apply the procedure provided in the agreement.
From this review of the aspects of the new agreement affecting the fn-;ff treatment of British goods imported into Canada, it will,

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
I think, be recognized that the Canadian government has succeeded in translating into policy those principles by which, in opposition, its leaders measured and criticized the C'awa agreement, of 1932. It will be remembered that the principal counts on which that agreement was then judged and found wanting were, first, that preference had been increased by raising rates against third countries instead of lowering them in favour of Britain; second, that an inordinate number of tariff rates were bound against decreases; and, third, that the term of the agreement-it was fixed for five years as against three for the new agreement-was unduly long and restricted the independence of action of succeeding parliaments and governments. Under each of these heads, the new agreement meets the conditions which the present Prime Minister laid down when leader of the opposition, and, taken as a whole, I think it can be regarded as the complement within the commonwealth to the United States trade agreement in the international field.
Turning now to those provisions of the new agreement bearing on the tariff treatment of Canadian goods imported into the United Kingdom, I need not emphasize the vital importance to Canada of confirming, for a further period of years, the assurance of unrestricted free entry into the United Kingdom market, which perhaps more than any other single factor has assisted Canadian economic recovery. In these years of constricted international trade, when high tariffs, exchange regulations and quantitative restrictions of every type have limited Canadian export opportunities, free entry into the United Kingdom market has saved the Canadian economy from strains that it probably could not have withstood. The importance of external markets to a country geared into a world economy needs no expounding- and of external markets no other has continued all through Canadian history to offer to the Canadian lumberman, farmer and fisherman the freedom of access which he enjoys in the United Kingdom.
The assurance in article I of the new agreement of the continuance of free entry for Canadian products is undoubtedly the great advantage which we receive from it. In maintaining free entry into the United Kingdom for Canadian goods, including manufactured products, we have kept open for a further term of years a door that once seemed to be rapidly closing. It is a matter of common knowledge that British industrial interests, with appetites edged by their recent taste of tariffs, are anxious to round out their present protective system by the imposition of duties on manufactured goods imported from Canada-nor
are British agriculturists by any means reconciled to the continuance of free entry for empire produce. The fact that, in spite of the influence of these powerful economic groups, the government of the United Kingdom were prepared to renew the assurance of free entry for Canadian produce is evidence of their appreciation of the magnitude and value of the reductions in duty on United Kingdom goods contained in schedule IV to the new agreement.
The trade figures that I am tabling in a separate document indicate much more clearly and vividly than any summary I could compress into this speech, the range of Canadian commodities, produce of factory, fisheries, forest, farms and mines, that are now being exported to the United Kingdom. It is this vast physical movement of goods that is in the last analysis the test of the value to Canada of the free entry into and preferential treatment in the world's greatest import market which the terms of this agreement assure us. We are all aware of the importance of the British market for lumber and salmon and apples and wheat-we are less likely to realize that it is also a market for iron and steel products-for motor cars and machinery, manufactured goods of many kinds. The exchange of goods between Canada and the United Kingdom is no longer merely an exchange of raw materials for finished goods.
I do not propose to enlarge on the items on which the United Kingdom has agreed to reduce or stabilize its tariffs. The reduction of duty and consequent increased margin of preference on natural silk stockings will be of value to an export industry that has, in recent years, been supplying an increasing share of the United Kingdom's import requirements, while the assurance that neither the duty on motor cars and their parts, nor their content qualification for preferential treatment, will be increased without the consent of the government of Canada will remove two sources of uncertainty which have caused a major export industry a great deal of anxiety. In passing, it might be noted that schedule II contains the first reduction of rates by the United Kingdom in a trade agreement with a commonwealth country; in most of the trade agreements concluded by the United Kingdom in recent years that country has refused to make any reductions in tariff, and confined its concessions to undertakings not to increase existing rates of duty.
As regards those commodities on which Canada is guaranteed the benefits of definite margins of preference, I might point out that there are no articles in schedule III on which
The Budget-Mr. Dunning

margins of preference were not bound in one or other of the agreements concluded by the United Kingdom with the dominions in 1932. There were a number of commodities on which the same margins were guaranteed to two or more dominions, and there were other commodities on which a margin was guaranteed to one dominion but of which some other dominion was actually the United Kingdom's largest supplier; for instance, the margin on honey was bound in the New Zealand agreement but Canada sent more honey to the United Kingdom than did New Zealand, while the margin on chilled and frozen salmon was bound in the Newfoundland agreement, although Canada was as large an exporter of this product as Newfoundland. In negotiating the present agreement, we not only consolidated the preferences shown in schedules B and C of the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, but added a number of preferences, which the United Kingdom was already bound to maintain and which are important to Canada.
Not only are no new commodities bound, but in no case have existing margins of preference been increased. It is as true to say for the United Kingdom as for Canada that no concessions incorporated in the new agreement have impaired the tariff treatment of third countries. In this connection, a point that is often overlooked by critics of the system of preferences might be emphasized. The preferences enjoyed by Canada in the United Kingdom market are really extremely moderate and are much lower in most cases than the measure of domestic protection enjoyed in home markets of foreign countries by competing producers of those commodities. The ad valorem preferences are as a rule ten per cent, and in no case exceed fifteen per cent; the preferences expressed as specific duties on foreign goods are approximately equivalent, at present prices, to this 'ange of ad valorem rates.
Article 5 falls into two parts-the first part, relating to bacon and hams, corresponds to article IV of the 1932 agreement, which assured free entry of bacon and ham up to a maximum of 2,500,000 hundredweight or 280,-
000.000 pounds per annum. The new agreement continues the assurance of free entry and confirms the maximum of two and a half million hundredweight (almost double the largest actual shipments made by Canada in any year to date). It assures Canadian farmers an uninterrupted opportunity of expanding their export trade toward that maximum and precludes the United Kingdom from

bringing imports from Canada within its general system of supply regulation, unless their rate of expansion becomes "abnormal and such as to endanger the effective working of the system of supply regulation"-and then only after consultation with the Canadian government, which, for its part, agrees to continue to furnish as close estimates as possible of the forward movements of bacon and bam to the United Kingdom market. The importance of the assurance of favourable entry into the profitable and protected British market for bacon-which is, incidentally, the only import market for bacon of any consequence in the world to-day-is clearly shown in the supplementary statistical material which I propose to have printed for the convenience of members of the house. At this time it is enough to say that in the last calendar year, out of total exports-that is Canadian exports-of bacon and ham of 158 million pounds, 98 per cent of the total, or more than 154 million pounds, valued in excess of $25,000,000, were shipped to the United Kingdom. The safeguarding of this market, and the maintenance of our opportunity to expand our sales in it, are in themselves major advantages of the new agreement.
The special provisions of the agreement relating to bacon and cattle represent an adjustment of differing types of economic organization. The general assurance of exemption from import duty had to be reinforced-for these commodities-by guarantees that the system of supply regulation which the government of the United Kingdom has adopted for the protection of its domestic agriculture would not frustrate the purpose of the preference which they were ready to accord to Canadian produce. It was, therefore, necessary in each case to work out in collaboration with the United Kingdom a method of securing for Canadian farmers the opportunity to develop their exports to the United Kingdom, without attempting to dictate to the United Kingdom government the form that its domestic policy should take. This method we think we have finally found in article 5 of the new agreement, which safeguards Canadian interests and at the same time enables the United Kingdom to proceed with a policy of marketing organization which they hope will result in stable and remunerative prices for bacon and beef, from which of course every Canadian producer of hogs and cattle will benefit.
The detailed arrangements affecting cattle and beef are complicated and I shall reserve their fuller discussion for committee. At this stage I shall only point out that our producers

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
are guaranteed absolute freedom from import duty, the value of which is enhanced by the preferential margin created by the imposition as from December 1, 1936, of a duty of a cent and a half a pound on foreign chilled beef, and a proportionate duty on foreign frozen beef. Within the framework of the general scheme for regulating the import of cattle and beef into the United Kingdom, Canadian exports of fat cattle and beef would be free from all quantitative control so long as the annual quantities shipped do not exceed what the agreement describes as "recent levels," that is, 1933 and 1934, when the number of fat cattle exported to the United Kingdom averaged 50,000 head as against 6,000 odd in 1935 and 33,000 in 1936. In passing I might point out that the irregular volume in which Canadian cattle move to the United Kingdom market, which in 1934 took 85 per cent of our exports as against only 7 per cent in the next year, illustrates the basic difficulty of adjusting our interest in reserving the right of access to what is now a secondary market for our cattlemen, with the United Kingdom's not unnatural interest in securing a stable and uninterrupted supply of meat from countries whose interest it would be to cooperate in its endeavours to stabilize supplies and prices at a remunerative level. In the light of this situation it should, I think, be agreed that the United Kingdom has gone a long way to recognize the special character of the Canadian cattle export trade and to make special allowances for its maintenance under the international meat scheme which it proposes to set up.
The fact that there is no counterpart in the present agreement to articles 5 and 18 of the 1932 agreement does not mean that the United Kingdom proposes to revert to the conditions which governed the importation of live cattle from Canada prior to 1932, or that Canada has any intention whatever of altering, to the disadvantage of the United Kingdom, the regulations for the importation of pedigreed stock from that country.
General considerations of the same order account for the disappearance of articles 10 to 17. Surely this country has sufficient interest in maintaining an efficient and law-abiding customs administration to make one-sided provisions, such as article 16 of the old agreement, entirely unnecessary. Questions of departmental procedure and organization, which are properly each country's domestic responsibility, have been returned to its jurisdiction. Formal changes of this character are of course subordinate to the main purposes of the agreement and will not involve any interruption of arrangements that have been working to the general satisfaction of both countries.
Concessions in the tariff treatment of United Kingdom goods which are to be made by Canada are chiefly those embodied in schedules IV and V to the agreement. Schedule IV enumerates the proposed reductions in duties, while schedule V sets forth such fixed margins of preference as the Canadian government undertakes to maintain in favour of certain specified commodities originating in the United Kingdom. For purposes of brevity and clarity, it is advisable to refer separately to these two schedules.
Schedule IV enumerates 425 tariff classifications of goods on which this country gives an undertaking not to increase duties of customs against Great Britain in excess of those therein set forth. Of the 425 items, 246 appear for the purpose of binding as a maximum the duty at present effective, and 179 for the purpose of reducing the existing rate on United Kingdom products. As an indication of the scope of the reductions in duty, it may be stated that, in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1936, imports from the United Kingdom of the goods covered by the group of 179 items which are to be reduced were valued at between 27 and 28 million dollars.

speechtext: Are the 179 items to be bound at the reduced rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Yes, bound against increase.
Obviously, time at my disposal will not permit detailed reference to the great number of commodities affected by the reductions in rate under schedule IV. Beyond any doubt, however, these represent the most extensive downward revision of duties on United Kingdom products made at any one time since the inception of the British preference. These reductions cover an extremely wide range of semi-processed and fully manufactured goods of the kind which enter into the daily living of our people:-
In foodstuffs and other edible commodities, reduced rates will apply on meat extracts, chocolate and cocoa preparations, unsweetened biscuits, pickled and preserved vegetables, marmalades and preserves, canned herring, and confectionery of all kinds. Reductions are proposed also on cigarettes, as well as on ale and beer.
A wide field of paper products is affected, including greeting cards, camera films, electrical insulating board, wall-papers, wrapping paper of all kinds, and "all manufactures of paper n.o.p.," including envelopes and stationery.
The Budget-Mr. Dunning

Paints, varnishes and lacquers, as well as white lead, oxides and fillers, will bear lower imposts on importation from the United Kingdom, as will also certain clay products, notably firebrick, earthenware churns and crocks, tiles and blocks for flooring, sanitary earthenware of all kinds, and various types of English-made stoneware and earthenware.
The duties on glass tableware, cut glassware, and certain sizes and weights of plate glass are lowered, and rates on all unenumerated manufactured articles of glass are also reduced.
Reductions will apply on numerous primary and secondary products of iron and steel, including hot- or cold-worked bars and rods; rounds and squares of defined sizes; hot-rolled strip and hoop steel; poundage and other alloy steels in flat \orm; corrugated metal sheets and enamelled iheets; saw steel, tempered; fully finished structural steel; forgings of iron or steel; railway axles; cast iron and cast steel pipe; wire cloth and netting, including netting for fox-fencing; coal-cleaning machinery; ore and rock crushers, grinding mills, coal cutters and rotary coal drills; blowers and rotary kilns for metallurgical purposes; office machinery of all kinds; vacuum cleaners and sewing machines; lawn mowers ind ball and roller bearings; nuts, bolts, butts ind hinges; vitreous enamelled ware and other kitchen and dairy hollow-ware; sanitary ware of iron or steel, coated or not; steel wheels for railway rolling stock; trackless trolley buses; aircraft engines; dynamos, transformers, generators and electric motors; electrical precision instruments of various kinds; files and rasps; buckles, clasps, fasteners, needles and pins; and furniture of wood or metal.
In cotton goods, the reductions will affect printed, dyed or coloured fabrics; shadow-cloth, gabardines and certain cut-pile fabrics; cotton handkerchiefs; book-binders' cloth, and certain fine cotton fabrics.
Practically all the major items in the wool schedule figure in the list of proposed reductions. The following wool products are among those which will enter from the United Kingdom at lower duties than heretofore; woollen and worsted yams, whether for manufacturing purposes or for counter-sale; pressed felt and wool filter cloth; blankets of all kinds; woollen and worsted fabrics "in the grey," imported for finishing in Canada; practically all lines and weights of woollen and worsted cloths, including suitings and overcoatings; woollen clothing of all kinds, and many unenumerated articles manufactured from or containing wool.
In silk and artificial silk goods there are many important reductions, including those

on woven fabrics of all kinds, embroideries, laces, braids and cords; and clothing and wearing apparel wholly or in part of artificial silk.
The duties are reduced on knitted garments, knitted underwear and knitted goods of all kinds; as well as on hosiery, gloves and mitts, rugs and carpets, and linoleum.
Leather and leather products show reductions on belting; on gloves and clothing leather; and on all leather further finished than tanned, n.o.p. Similarly, duties are reduced on boots and shoes; on trunks, bags and valises; on fancy cases and boxes, and on clothing made from India rubber or from water-proofed cotton fabrics.
Miscellaneous articles upon which reduced rates are proposed includes braces, jewellery, brushes of all kinds, pens and pencils, tobacco pipes and all smokers' accessories, photographic dry plates, abrasives, medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations, toilet soaps, mucilage and adhesive pastes, surgical dressings and bandages, manufactured goods of celluloid, halibut liver oil, blackings and dressings for leather or metal, articles of sterling or other silverware, clock movements and parts thereof, children's carriages and sleds, picture and photograph frames, and woven dress linens.
An interesting feature is the provision for the free entry, from the United Kingdom, of goods, other than spirits or wines, more than 100 years old.
The undertaking to maintain certain fixed margins of preference applies only to the items enumerated in schedule V, which sets forth in each instance the measure or amount of the margin. This schedule contains 91 items as against 215 in schedule E of the agreement of 1932; moreover, in 21 of the 91 items comprising the schedule the amount of the margin to be maintained is materially lessened. Among the 125 items upon which Canada is no longer (as compared with 1932) bound to maintain fixed margins of preference, are many which will be of great value in trade negotiations likely to be entered into with other countries. There is this further important difference between Canada's commitments as to fixed margins in 1932 and the commitments being entered into to-day: that, except as regards certain primary iron and steel commodities, by far the greater part of the scheduled items enumerate commodities not produced or manufactured commercially at all in Canada, and, hence, entail no element of protection for domestic interests. The value of imports from the United Kingdom,

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
in the fiscal year 1936, under the 91 items on which fixed margins have been granted, was approximately 37 million dollars.
In the tariff resolutions which I shall table on concluding, it is provided that the various rates set upon United Kingdom products, under this agreement, shall become British preferential rates in the customs tariff. This is in accordance with the practice followed for many years by Canada of generalizing within the empire to the greatest possible extent concessions in tariff treatment granted to any one empire country. This principle is so desirable that, in this instance, the government is disposed to apply it without exception, in spite of the fact that there are involved one or two items in respect of which the chief beneficiary may be an empire country which affords no preference to Canada; in such instances, it lies within the power of the governor-general in council to withdraw from any such non-reciprocating empire country the preferential treatment now voluntarily extended to it.
We regard the agreement as a friendly arrangement for closer economic cooperation, from which both countries will benefit and by which no other country will suffer. A liberal and moderate preferential policy such as this agreement embodies will supplement and strengthen the growing movement for freer trade within the world as a whole.
Other tariff proposals, not directly associated with the United Kingdom agreement, while not great in number, are of importance to Canadian producing and consuming interests, and of considerable significance to countries whose trade with Canada has been a factor in the recovery to which I have previously referred. Revisions m duties which extend to intermediate tariff countries include reductions in the rates on cotton clothing of all kinds, as well as on a wide range of articles manufactured from cotton; on various gums and resins used in industrial processes; on well-casing of steel for oil and gas wells; on printing plates and paper used in the production of periodicals; on parts for aircraft engines; on a wide range of plastics and plastic materials; on plate glass, decorative marble, slipper cloth, parts of surgical instruments, and certain copper alloys. Provision is made for the entry free of duties from all countries of small "personal gifts," as well as for the free entry of stringed musical instruments certified to be more than 100 years old. Various liquorice fibres and products will enter at lower rates than heretofore, as will various fumigants and disinfectants, egg-cleaning machines, electric razors, forged steel rolls,
silk yarns covered with metallic strip, certain motion-picture equipment, corset rivets, and cotton laces used in the garment industry.

speechtext:
Reports which have been received from the tariff board and which find reflection in the tariff resolutions moved to-day include those on cherries in solution, motion-picture equipment, steel wool, hard rubber in sheets, and plastics, the last named providing for a completely new schedule to cover these products, now so widely used in industry. The board has reported also as regards chiffons and silica sand; and all reports received I shall table this day. The board will have ready in the near future reports on other matters referred to it, and it is expected that these will be received in time for consideration by the government while the house is still in committee of ways and means.
Conclusion	.
May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, on a note of cheer and of challenge: cheer, because the immediate outlook points to a continuation of the encouraging trends in economic activity which I have already reported; challenge, because the problems of depression we have still to solve and the new problems which will emerge with buoyant prosperity demand the best that we are capable of in wisdom, in forethought and in cooperative endeavour. We may rejoice that we have been among the leaders in the degree of our recovery from the depths of depression. But we have special problems inherited from the war or arising out of our economic and political structure with which we as a people and as a parliament will be confronted for some time to come. These problems are by no means insuperable; they merely forbid complacency, sectional dissension or relaxation of effort.
They can and will be solved as prosperity incresses, if only we take care to see that such prosperity is soundly based and evenly distributed, and if we all put our shoulders to the wheel in a common national effort. I mention them here not to diminish the joy which we naturally feel in the record of expanding trade, increasing business activity, rising payrolls and improving revenues which I have been able to report, but rather as a challenge to continued endeavour, to individual, corporate and national integrity, to a keener sense of trusteeship in carrying out our everyday business and civic responsibilities. If this challenge be accepted by the Canadian people, I am confident, sir, that better days lie ahead-better indeed than we have yet known.
The Budget-Mr. Dunning

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext:
On Friday, February 12.
when this item was being considered, I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) a question concerning the attitude of the department in connection with the dismissal of certain returned men and also the non-appointment of returned men to vacancies that had occurred, and I called particular attention to the case of the dismissal of the postmaster at Canterbury Station, New Brunswick. I pointed out to the minister at that time that a request had been made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Clark) for the dismissal of the postmaster on the ground that he had been engaged in partisan work during the previous election. I also pointed out that an affidavit had been sent to the department but that evidently it was not considered sufficient. The department had its inspector go to Canterbury Station from the
Supply-Post Office

city of Saint John; an investigation was held, not of the charge of partisanship but in regard to the site of the post office, and the postmaster was dismissed on the ground that the site was not as good as another which was proposed. In this connection I wish to quote from certain letters that passed between officials of the Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League, and others, and the department. In reply to a letter from the hon. member for York-Sunbury complaining about partisanship, the Postmaster General, on April 1, 1936, wrote:
Dear Mr. Clark:
With reference to your communication of the 27th March in regard to the position of postmaster at Canterbury Station, N.B., I may say there is no vacancy in the postmastership at that point at the present time and no serious complaints have been received about the manner in which the post office is being conducted by the present incumbent. Thomas J. McMullin, who was appointed on the 12th January, 1931.
1 note your remarks to the effect that charges of political partisanship can easily be sustained against the present postmaster.
Charges of partisanship were not investigated, but the postmaster was dismissed, as I have said, on the ground that the site was not satisfactory. I would point out to the Postmaster General that in the correspondence set out in sessional paper 118, it appears that as far as the site was concerned there is very little difference between the previous site and the proposed site, the latter being about one hundred yards farther away from the centre of the village. The village is a very small one, and the previous site is nearer the school. As we all know, in these small villages and country districts children go to the post offices and get most of the mail.
Communications were received by the department from returned soldiers' organizations. On page 13 of this sessional paper is a copy of a telegram sent to the Postmaster General from the Federicton branch of the Canadian Legion. The telegram reads:
Hon. J. C. Elliott,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Out.
Strongly protest removal of Thomas McMullin ex-service man from postmastership Canterbury.
W. A. Gibson,
President, Canterbury branch.
In the sessional paper is included another telegram from the Woodstock branch of the Canadian Legion, as follows:
Woodstock, N.B.. June 9.
Hon. J. C. Elliott,
Postmaster General,.
Ottawa, Ont.
Thomas J. McMullin postmaster Canterbury York county, N.B. to-day received notice of dismissal no reason given from post office inspector St. John said dismissal to take

effect twelfth instant. This man is returned soldier receives small pension and is member this branch. Special meeting executive called this evening strongly protest this dismissal and ask new appointment held up pending investigation.
On June 12 the appointment was made. On page 9 of the sessional paper is a letter from J. C. G. Herwig, of the service bureau of the Canadian Legion at Ottawa, reading as follows:
The Hon. J. C. Elliott, K.C., M.P.,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa. Ontario.
Dear Mr. Elliott:
An urgent request has been received from our Woodstock (N.B.), branch to make representations to you with reference to the release of Thomas J. McMullin of Canterbury. I quote hereunder from their message.
The message is the same as the telegram I have just read.
This notice -was given without much warning and no reason was given for the dismissal which is to take effect from the 12th instant.
It is pointed out that Mr. McMullin is a returned soldier receiving a small pension and the postmastership, therefore, is his livelihood because pension is insufficient for maintenance. I understand from officers of your department that the reason for this dismissal is that the present location of the office is unsatisfactory. If this is the case, then we feel that McMullin should be given an opportunity to change to a more suitable location before his dismissal is carried out.
When discussing the release of returned soldiers with you, you gave us assurance that they would not be removed from positions of this kind except for cause. In this case we are assured that the objection could be readily met by Mr. McMullin if he were given an opportunity to do so.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give me the date of that letter?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext:
The letter was written on June 10. It continues:
We think, therefore, that we are not unreasonable in asking that you delay drastic action in this case until Mr. McMullin has an opportunity of providing more suitable quarters.
This was not done. McMullin was dismissed on June 12.
I want to bring to the minister's attention another matter that has to do with the actions of certain commissions appointed to investigate partisanship in New Brunswick. The one case I refer to particularly is the dismissal of a postmaster at Mill Cove, New Brunswick, which is in my own constituency. This case is entirely different from the other. As I pointed out, in the first case the postmaster was accused of partisanship. He was dismissed on the ground that the site was not considered satisfactory. That was the excuse given. In the second case the ground on

Supply-Post Office
which the complainant asked for the postmaster's dismissal was that the site was not satisfactory, but it was so obvious that the site proposed was unsatisfactory-not as satisfactory as the former site-that a charge of partisanship was brought against him and an investigation was held. The complaint was made by the defeated candidate in the constituency of Royal. He wrote to the department, who advised him how the investigation was to be carried out. Affidavits were made and a commissioner was appointed to hold the investigation. The commissioner was the law partner of the man who made the complaint, Mr. White, the defeated candidate in Royal. In order that the minister may understand this matter, I shall quote from some of the correspondence.
On June 3, a letter was written to the Postmaster General as follows:
June 3, 1936.
Hon. J. C. Elliott,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Re: Mill Cove Post Office Dear Mr. Elliott:
I would request the removal of the above post office from C. W. Orchard's to James McLaughlin's, as location of the office on McLaughlin's premises would be a more practical site to enable it to better serve its patrons. The present site is not, I understand, as satisfactory as if the office were located on Mr McLaughlin's premises.
Yours very truly,
Donald V. White.
As a matter of fact the proposed location at Mr. McLa'ughlin's would require the patrons of that post office to walk about an extra mile for their mail, and when the matter was looked into it was found that the complaint that the site was unsatisfactory would not hold water; so then it was decided to bring a charge of partisanship against the holder of the office. An affidavit was procured from a gentleman named Robert M. Mott. I shall not read the whole of it, but his chief charge was:
In the last dominion election I saw the said C. W. Orchard drive up in his car with a Conservative voter to one of the polling booths in the said parish of Cambridge and in the afternoon I saw his wife drive to the polls with two Conservative women in her car.
The department wrote to Mr. Orchard asking him what he had to say about the charge, and he replied:
June 30, 1936.
Postmaster General,
Ottawa,
Canada.
Dear Sir:
In reply to your letter of the 22nd I will say as to my taking an active part in politics it is a complete falsehood. I did not canvass nor was I canvassed. True I took my wife's
uncle along with me to the polling booth he came and asked my wife if he could get a chance with me-he has been a life long Liberal-he says I don't say how I'm going to vote, she said that is your own affair there is room if you want to go. On my way back my wife's cousin asked me if she and my wife's niece could go along with my wife, her cousin has always been Liberal don't know about her niece what she is. We did not ask any of them to go with either of us, they came back with other parties. On her way my wife took a man in whom afterward we heard refused to go in the Conservative cars. She asked him if he would have a drive he accepted. With the exception of asking this man to have a drive we can both swear that we only took these people because we were asked-and did no canvassing whatever. I want the name of the persons who sent in the sworn statement-how could anyone take an oath that these people were either Liberal or Conservative.
There have been a number of falsehoods about our office which we have proved out to the department and it is getting irksome. I hope I shall always keep broadminded enough that I can give a person a lift regardless of their politics in which I take no active part.
Please write me the name of the person who sent the statement.
Yours truly,
Charles W. Orchard.
A commission was appointed and an investigation held. I shall read the report. The investigation was held at Cambridge, New Brunswick, on September 24, 1936, and the evidence as reported reads:
The witnesses for the informant testified that during the provincial and dominion election campaigns of 1935 Charles W. Orchard, postmaster at Mill Cove, attended the conventions of one of the political parties, that during the federal campaign Mr. Orchard attended a political meeting of the same party on the evening when two of the parties held meetings in the district, and that during his term of office Mr. Orchard had attended other political conventions of the same party. They also testified that on dominion election day, October 14. 1935, Mr. Orchard had driven one votei to the polls at Cambridge, and that his wife had driven two women voters to the same poll.
The postmaster gave evidence on his own behalf, stating that he had not attended political conventions as a delegate, that voters driven to the polls were driven at their own request, and were taken by his wife and himself when they themselves went to vote. He admitted that he had never attended conventions of other than the one party, but stated that he had attended joint nomination some years ago and that during the 1935 dominion election campaign he had attended a political meeting of another party.
The evidence was to the effect that it was a Liberal meeting.
His wife, deputy postmistress, testified similarly regarding the voters driven to the polls, as well as voters themselves, two of whom claimed to belong to party other than the one the postmaster was believed to support. All the voters transported were relatives of Mrs. Orchard. The honorary chairman of the Conservative party for the district testified that postmaster Orchard had never attended committee meetings of that party.
Supply-Post Office

The finding of the commission was:
In view of the evidence submitted, I feel that sufficient proof has been offered to find postmaster Orchard guilty of acts of political partisanship.
The convention which he was accused of attending was an open-air convention held on the shores of Grand lake in the county of Queens, New Brunswick. Hundreds of people were there and I saw among them the chairman of the Liberal party in the county of Queens, and dozens of other Liberals. Mr. Orchard lives only a few miles from this place, and practically everyone in the neighbourhood, no matter what might be his party affiliations, attended this convention. It was like a picnic, but only those wfio were delegates could vote. Mr. Orchard was dismissed on this very flimsy evidence which was brought before this commission. The facts proved were that he conveyed three voters to the polls; two of these voters were Liberals and they do not know how the third voted. I should like to read to the committee one or two letters indicating the attitude of the public. This may seem trivial to some, but it is important to the people who live in this district, and that is why I am bringing it to the attention of the Postmaster General. I am not going to worry the committee in regard to these commissions which have been investigating not only this case but others, but I know of other dismissals in my own constituency just as unfair and unreasonable as this one. I hope in future these matters will be more carefully considered by the authorities. I have in my hand many letters but I shall read just a few. This one is dated September 27, 1936:
Bear Sir:
As I am a resident of Mill Cove I am writing to you in regard to the post office. There are five families living here and the post office is one and a half miles away. I think it is far enough to have to walk after the mail without haring to walk any further. If they shift the post office we will have to walk for our mail two miles and a half. So I don't know what we will do. Please let me know what is to be done.
Another letter, dated September 24. reads:
Just a few lines in regard to the office at Charlie Orchards. As I think it would be an unfair thing to move the post office any further than where it is for we have about one mile now and what will it be for us if you moved it any further so hope you will please decide to leave it at Charlie Orchard for the people in the settlement, and obliging.
Mrs. Clifford Thompson.
The point is that practically all the people who get their mail at this post office were

compelled to walk a mile further for their mail just to satisfy a supporter of the party in power. I may also point out that the post office of which Mr. Orchard was postmaster was beside the school at Mill Cove and the children who come from the back districts would get their mail and take it home after school. After the post office was moved, they had to go half a mile up the road to McLaughlin's, get their mail, go back half a mile and then return home. Anyone who knows country districts in the winter will know that is a real hardship. I hope that in the matter of appointing commissions to investigate complaints of this kind there will be more careful investigation, and that the rights of the people will be the first consideration. It does not make so much difference that Orchard was dismissed, but the fact that dozens of people have to walk daily another mile through all kinds of weather to get their mail seems very unfair.
I should like to correct a statement I made the other day with reference to the postmastership in the town of Woodstock. I stated that a returned man had not been appointed to that vacancy. That is correct, but I have learned that the present incumbent is appointed only in a temporary capacity. But I object to that. Looking over some records not long ago, I noted that most of these temporary appointments are given to some party heeler, and then perhaps later a returned man is appointed. Why cannot the returned man be appointed as temporary postmaster in the first instance? It is sometimes months before the regular appointment is made. I ask the Postmaster General if it is the intention of his department to appoint a returned man to the Woodstock post office. If so. how soon will that appointment be made? It has been pending now for a considerable length of time and it seems to me the appointment should be made without further delay.
I also asked the Postmaster General last year with reference to the post office at Florenceville, New Brunswick. A widow was dismissed from that post office without very much reason, as is the case in a good many instances in my province. At that time I asked the Postmaster General: "If a change is contemplated, will an investigation be made before any such change takes place?" The Postmaster General answered:	"Yes,
an investigation will be made." But I am informed that no investigation was made, that the postmistress was dismissed without any investigation. The Postmaster General gave me his word that an investigation would be held, but there was no investigation.

Supply-Post Office

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext:
Dealing first with the Canterbury office, since the hon. member started speaking I have been able to obtain the report upon which this change was made. This office is in the electoral district of York-Sunbury. The revenue was SI,834. A report was asked from the district director, and I have a copy of it in my hand. It is dated April 27, 1936, and reads:
A number of the patrons of the office were interviewed, and it would appear that public opinion was favourable to the proposed location. The proposed site is 180 yards west of the present location and is more central as shown by the sketch herewith enclosed, which also shows the location of tile patrons.
I should be glad to elaborate on that if my hon. friend wishes me to do so.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: I should like to ask a question. In the letter written by the Postmaster General to Mr. Herwig on June 10, a statement was made to the effect that a returned soldier in a position of this kind would not be dismissed without cause. I also understand that Mr. McMullin was not given an opportunity to change the site of his post office, so in my opinion the reason given was only an excuse. Be that as it may, however, I should like to ask the minister if Mr. McMullin was given an opportunity to change the site of the post office, if it was not satisfactory.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: I can go only by the records I have before me. First, I might say a word with regard to the question of changing the site of a post office in charge of a returned soldier. If a change of site is considered desirable, the practice has been, quite consistently for a number of years, to have an examination made by the district director. If this report shows conclusively that some other site is much more desired by the people who are to be served, which site according to the map is much more central- and it was so in this instance-the change is made. It has not been the practice to consider the returned soldier as being dismissed if his site is not as suitable as the other one suggested. That is not in the nature of a dismissal for cause.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: I should like to ask another question. Did the Postmaster General receive any complaints with regard to this site prior to the letter which was written by the hon. member for York-Sunbury? I have the correspondence under my hand, and it does not indicate any such complaint.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext:
I am not aware of any such complaint, but this change was made at the request of the patrons who
were being served, and with a view to securing a better site.
Now I might say a word with regard to the second matter to which my hon. friend referred, the post office at Mill Cove. I have before me the finding of the investigator, and I would say to my hon. friend that I think quite as much care has been taken in these cases as has been customary in regard to matters of this kind. A commissioner was appointed; he made a report, and the report indicates that the postmaster at that point has been guilty of political partisanship. I should like to refer my hon. friend to what is frequently the most important evidence one gets. It is the evidence of the postmaster himself as to whether or not he was guilty of political partisanship. This is what he says:
The postmaster gave evidence on his own behalf, stating that he had not attended political conventions as a delegate, that voters driven to the polls were driven at their own request, and were taken by his wife and himself when they themselves went to vote.
In all fairness I would suggest to my hon. friend that most people are taken to the polls by their friends when their friends go to vote.
He admitted that he had never attended conventions of other than the one party, but stated that he had attended joint nomination some years ago and that during the 1935 dominion election campaign he had attended a political meeting of another party. His wife, deputy postmistress, testified similarly regarding the voters driven to the polls, as well as voters themselves, two of whom claimed to belong to party other than the one the postmaster was believed to support.
I want to say to my hon. friend that, apart altogether from the evidence given by the postmaster, the finding of the commissioner is that on the whole evidence given before him the postmaster was guilty of political partisanship. I do not know how we can retry the finding of any commissioner as long as the record appears to show that there was evidence which, if believed by him, would support the charge. I am not going to argue the matter, but that has been the practice, and that is the course which was followed in this case.
Now I should like to say a word with regard to Woodstock, about which my hon. friend asked. The revenue of that post office is over 819,000. When the appointment is made it will undoubtedly have to be made by the civil service commission, and the returned soldier preference will apply. I am afraid I cannot say much more than my hon. friend can say with regard to what the civil service commission will do. I think that covers the three cases to which my hon. friend referred.
Supply-Post Office

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext:
This is a public utility, Mr. Chairman, and in my opinion it should be operated in a different way. I do not intend to say very much about this firing business. I remember when the present Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) was on my football team; I believe this is a little contrary to his own way of doing business, so I do not believe he has very much to do with it, though there were postmasters fired in the Niagara peninsula.
This utility is maintained by the public and should be conducted on a commercial basis if we are to have any efficiency. Years ago Sir William Mulock got efficiency and many reforms were introduced into the department in order to make it more businesslike. I must say, however, that this business of firing aged employees who are in the evening of life, without making any provision for them, is not creditable to the post office or any other public utility.
I come from a city which contributes some $7,000,000 yearly to the postal revenues of this country, and in my opinion Toronto is getting very poor service for the amount of money expended. In the residential districts the service is not what it should be. In addition to that, I believe Toronto, which contributes about $90,000,000 annually to the revenues of this country, should have some better post office terminal system. In that city we have no post office with the exception of the old building which was constructed shortly after confederation, at the head of Toronto street. It is true that we have the terminal in the union station, but I maintain that the Post Office Department < f Canada is away behind the times. We are sending ministers over to England on almost every boat nowadays. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was in the house for only three months before he took a Cook's tour around Europe. If they would open their eyes and see what the British post office is doing in the way of efficiency, they would be doing something for the people of this country.
As a postal item is under discussion, I should like to know what the department is going to do about the postal service in my constituency, that of Broadview, which comprises a large district over the Don, and in which is one of the largest business retail streets in Canada, namely, Danforth. In that section of Toronto there is no adequate post office. Post office business is conducted in an old leased building. Other places, from which the department derives very little revenue, can have buildings valued at $100,000 erected. Only the other day we heard about one at

Fort Erie, in the Niagara district, where the revenue is not nearly as large as it would be in Toronto. I do not object to Fort Erie getting something, but the commencement of that federal building with the laying of the corner stone was nothing but a Liberal rally in the district. With a golden trowel the member laid the corner stone, and there were the usual ceremonies. The revenues from that district are set out in the returns received by the Postmaster General.
In my opinion the Post Office Department should be operated from the commercial aspect, and the commercial aspect only. There should be some efficiency in the department. Toronto contributes $7,000,000 to the revenue. In that city we are entitled to one cent drop letters. The revenue from Toronto should not be used, to the detriment of increased service for Toronto at less cost, to bolster up post offices in other places throughout Canada, in the manner indicated.
All along the line the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, which contribute eighty per cent of the cash taxation to the federal treasury, have been discriminated against. The day is coming when the businessmen will insist upon business administration in the Post Office Department. We should have additional facilities in Toronto for handling the mail. Regarding the delivery of letters in the residential districts of Toronto may I refer to an editorial appearing in the North Toronto Herald, published in the constituency of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Baker). I happen to live in that district. In the newspaper editorial there is a complaint about several postmen having been bitten by dogs when they go to deliver the mail. That should not be so. The minister ought to notify people that if they want to have mad dogs, and that kind of thing, about the property, they had better get their mail at the post office.
This is not the only public utility in Toronto which is suffering thus from vicious dogs attacking inspectors. The minister is not much of a dog fancier-at least he was not when I used to know him so well. May I repeat that other public utilities in Toronto are suffering in the same way from people who keep these mad or semi-mad dogs. When postmen come to deliver letters they are bitten, and they have no remedy for damages.
In addition to that, the time is not far distant when more humane methods should be used for the good of the rank and file of the men who do the work in the Post Office Department,-not for the brass hats to whom the hon. member for Temiscouata referred.

Supply-Post Office
The rank and file of postmen are not receiving the consideration they should. Should one of these poor chaps steal a dollar or a dollar and a half out of the mail, he may be sent to prison for three years. I know of no other public utility which uses its employees in that way; when such utilities have revenues, they pay their employees proper living wages and rates. In my view the law concerning the three year sentence in connection with postal employees should be changed.
Some of these postmen are returned men. One of them may steal a dollar or two out of a letter, especially if his family is not receiving proper maintenance. With the increased revenues in the Post Office Department I say that law should be changed. It was introduced before confederation, and there should be some amendment of it, and the men affected given parole or some other consideration.
There is another point concerning the revenue of the department about which I should like to speak. The newspapers of Canada are receiving a cash subsidy of $8,000,000 from parliament. Why do they receive that? They get it through the carrying of second class mail at less than cost. The special freight rate they enjoy is greatly to their benefit, and it costs the department a loss of over $8,000,000 to carry the newspapers through the mail. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) is one who knows a great deal about the Post Office Department, and only a few days ago he referred to this matter. If these newspapers can afford to have a couple of pages of turf news, they can afford to pay a proper rate for the delivery of their newspapers, and to do it without cash subsidies from parliament. In my view the law in that regard should be changed.
The Postmaster General should take up the bill I introduced some years ago concerning the identity of the newspaper as to ownership. We should follow the law of Great Britain and that of the United States, whereby newspapers must disclose their identity as to ownership, stockholders, mortgagees, mergers and matters of that kind or be refused the right of the mails. The fourth estate is not what it used to be as a defender of public rights or of the liberty of the subject; this seems to be past and gone, forever. I say that the Postmaster General should consider this matter and bring in an amendment to the Post Office Act, whether hon. gentlemen in another chamber like it or not. There should be proper disclosures as to ownership of newspapers receiving these subsidies; otherwise they should be denied the right to use the mail, as is done in Washington, under the laws of the United States.
I believe the department should add new features. I hope the Postmaster General will go to England for the coronation ceremonies, because if he goes over there and keeps his eyes open-and he has pretty good eyes when he wants to see-he will notice the improvements they have in England. The minister sometimes did not see the referee and got ruled off when on my team, but he is very observant. I believe he should go to England and see what the Post Office Department over there is doing to add to the usefulness of the post office.
The Post Office Department has not in Toronto the modern facilities to do business. It is not equipped as are other public utilities, such as the Bell Telephone Company, the Consumers' Gas Company or the Hydro Electric. It has not the modern type of building, modern facilities or modern methods. The Post Office Department is a public utility, and as such it is away behind the times. We could learn a lot by going to Washington and finding out what they are doing in the larger cities of the United States.
I agree with the hon. member for Parkdale in connection with his observations about the Christmas mail. When hon. members on this side were in office they played the game. I never succeeded in placing a man in the Post Office Department at Christmas time. I never asked to, because I knew it would not be done. Last Christmas the returned soldiers got a raw deal from the Post Office Department. They were asked to file their applications, go down to Adelaide street and register. They spent hours and hours of time trying to get the work, but they were refused. Other men from all over Ontario were taken on. I do not blame the present Postmaster General or the Toronto postmaster, but I believe there should be in Toronto a system similar to that found in the municipalities. Municipalities try to run their business from a commercial standpoint, and not as Liberals or Conservatives. If the federal authorities did as the municipalities do, they would get greater efficiency in the Post Office Department, and would receive a fair day's work for a fair day's pay from the rank and file of the men who, dear knows, could stand a little increase in their pay. We should have more humane treatment of the men. Some day the people who pay for the Post Office Department will rise up and have something to say about the way in which it has been operated.

The rest of us sit at home and enjoy ourselves, and I think these humble employees of the Post Office Department should have the same privilege as their fellow citizens.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT

As far as these services are concerned, I cannot add anything to what I said when the matter was under discussion for a considerable length of time the other evening. The result of the present arrangement has been exceedingly favourable, particularly in the large cities. Communications we have received from various sources indicate how much the people in those places appreciate getting their Christmas mail either on Christmas day or within a day or two of Christmas. I repeat what I said the other evening that with regard to Christmas it is utterly impossible, particularly in the large cities, to keep anywhere in sight of the work if we allow the complete Christmas holiday to pass without the mail being sorted or any mail being served; it could not be finished at the end of the week. That has been the experience in the past. We in the department are most anxious to give the public the best possible service consistent with reasonable expenditure. Nobody desires less than I do to pay out money to give people service they do not want, but at the same time we owe something not only to the people to whom the letters are delivered but to those who have sent those letters; they are entitled to have them delivered within a reasonable length of time. With regard to smaller places it is much easier to make some arrangements which may not be so ex-

Supply-Post Office

pensive but will give a reasonable service. We are surveying the whole situation, but I should not be fair to my hon. friend if I led him to believe I thought that, with a volume of mail such as we had this last year, it would be humanly possible, if we were to dispense with the Christmas mail delivery, to get the Christmas mail disposed of within the succeeding three or four days.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: As reference has been made to large cities, may I point out that I understand that in the city of Quebec, which is quite a large place, the people are opposed to these deliveries. As regards accumulation of mail for delivery on Christmas day, a little missionary work could be done by means of advertising so that people would be induced to mail their communications earlier. The department very thoughtfully sent us circulars early in December telling us that, if we wanted to have our mail delivered to the United Kingdom or elsewhere abroad, it should be posted by a certain date. The same procedure might be applied to deliveries within Canada. What I had in mind was the interests of the postmen. As I have said, all of us enjoy Christmas and New Year's day, and I believe these employees should be with their families on those occasions. maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: May I inquire if representations have been made through the postal services, particularly in cities of 25.000 to 40,000 population, asking that Saturday afternoons be allowed to the employees who work in those cities? Very many of these men are interested in sports. It seems to me that while the argument advanced by the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) may be quite in keeping with the situation as far as Christmas mail is concerned, it is difficult to appreciate the necessity of having mail delivered on Saturday afternoons in these smaller places, where half the places of business are closed. I understand that strong representations in this connection are being made.

Prior to the recent inauguration of service on Saturday afternoons, no mails which were received in a city like Montreal after about nine o'clock in the morning were delivered that day, and numerous complaints, verbal and written, were received. maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM TRADE AGREEMENT- INSTRUCTION TO COMMITTEE OP WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER AND REPORT
speechtext: If my hon. friend had just borne with me a moment I do not think it would have been necessary for him to ask the last question, because what applies to the city of Montreal as regards mail that is sent part of the way by air applies also to these smaller cities. If this mail comes in on a Saturday morning after sortations are made for the mail carriers to get out on their rounds, it lies in the post office until the following Monday morning. The delaying of one letter of that kind will do more injury to the Post Office Department than can be cured by a lot of expenditure and much diligence. That is our trouble. Unless there is a sortation, a staff kept for sortation purposes on Saturday morning, and the mail that comes in on Saturday morning is sorted so as to get out on Saturday afternoon, all that mail remains over until the following Monday, and the result in some cases, particularly where important business messages are involved, is very serious.
